introduction: These readings define 'the world' and warn against it. The world, Bahá’u’lláh says, is whatever turns a person aside from God; it is a shadow, a day, a delusion that has intoxicated most people with desire, wealth and ease; ‘Abdu’l-Bahá adds that the world of nature holds people at the level of the animal and that kings and conquerors leave nothing behind. A few passages draw the line carefully: wealth and the good things of the earth are not themselves the world. A hundred of the guide's three hundred quotations are read here, ten from each tenth of the reading order, beside a hundred from elsewhere. Most stand alongside, for the theme is common ground: Ecclesiastes, the Gospels on mammon and the rich fool, the Qur'an on play and pastime, Paul, the Dhammapada, Seneca, Plato's cave, Wordsworth, Thoreau, Thomas à Kempis. Fourteen push back or add a side: Genesis and the Wisdom of Solomon on a world God made and loves, Nietzsche's 'remain true to the earth', Tagore, Herrick and Khayyam on delight, Hopkins and Elizabeth Barrett Browning on nature charged with God, Marx on religion as opium, Milton against cloistered virtue, the good Samaritan, and Jesus's prayer that his disciples be kept in the world.
questions: 'By the world is meant that which turneth you aside from Him.' What, by that definition, is the world for you, and what is not?
Someone in the readings asks why we should cut ourselves off from a world God created. How do the readings answer, and how do Genesis, Paul and the Wisdom of Solomon?
Nietzsche asked people to remain true to the earth; Marx called religion an opium. What in these readings would they object to, and what might they miss?
Hopkins and Browning see the world charged with God. Is that the opposite of detachment, or its fruit?
The readings say the world has 'intoxicated' most people. What does sobriety look like in a working life?
Milton would not praise a cloistered virtue. Where do the readings ask for engagement with the world?

outside.why: The first letter of John says: love not the world, neither the things that are in the world.
Jesus prayed for his disciples not that they be taken out of the world, but kept from the evil. How is one in the world and not of it?
Shakespeare's Prospero says the great globe itself shall dissolve like a pageant, and that we are such stuff as dreams are made on.
Genesis says that God saw every thing that he had made, and behold, it was very good. Is the questioner in the reading wrong to ask what the world is for?
Paul writes that every creature of God is good, and nothing to be refused if it be received with thanksgiving. What separates use of the world from attachment to it?
Jesus told a rich young man to sell what he had and give to the poor, and he went away sorrowful.
A king in Ecclesiastes looks on all the works his hands had wrought, and finds all vanity and vexation of spirit.
The Qur'an draws the same line: seek the abode of the Hereafter, and neglect not thy portion of the world.
Seneca wrote that it is not the man who has too little, but the man who craves more, that is poor.
Jesus said that no man can serve two masters: ye cannot serve God and mammon.
Bunyan's dream begins as he walks through the wilderness of this world.
Paul speaks of those who worshipped and served the creature more than the Creator.
The Dhammapada says there is no fire like passion, and no happiness higher than rest.
In the parable of the sower some seed is choked with cares and riches and pleasures of this life, and brings no fruit to perfection.
The Buddha's fire sermon says the same of the whole of experience: the eye is aflame, forms are aflame.
Paul warns that the love of money is the root of all evil, and that those who covet it pierce themselves with many sorrows.
Zhuangzi says the perfect man uses his mind as a mirror: it responds to what is before it, but does not retain it.
Pascal says that man is neither angel nor brute, and that whoever would act the angel acts the brute.
Jesus said that the light of the body is the eye: if thine eye be single, thy whole body shall be full of light.
Wordsworth complained that the world is too much with us: getting and spending, we lay waste our powers.
Jesus told Nicodemus that what is born of the flesh is flesh, and what is born of the Spirit is spirit.
A psalm says that man in honour who understands not is like the beasts that perish.
Nietzsche's Zarathustra implores his hearers to remain true to the earth and distrust those who speak of superearthly hopes. What would he say the reading takes from people?
Paul tells the Colossians to set their affection on things above, not on things on the earth.
Hopkins found the world of nature charged with the grandeur of God. Is nature a darkness to be born out of, or a place where glory is seen?
James asks what our life is: a vapour that appears for a little time, and then vanishes away.
Shelley's king of kings left a boast on a pedestal, and round it the lone and level sands.
Marcus Aurelius observed that Alexander the Macedonian and his groom were brought by death to the same state.
A psalmist had seen the wicked in great power, spreading like a green bay tree; yet he passed away and could not be found.
The rich man in the parable told his soul to take its ease; God said to him, this night thy soul shall be required.
The Preacher begins with the same question: vanity of vanities; what profit hath a man of all his labour?
The Apocalypse answers a church that says 'I am rich and have need of nothing': thou art poor, and blind, and naked.
A prayer in Proverbs asks for neither poverty nor riches, but food convenient for me.
Paul describes the apostles as poor, yet making many rich; as having nothing, and yet possessing all things.
In Luke's Gospel Jesus says simply: blessed be ye poor, for yours is the kingdom of God.
Proverbs warns that riches make themselves wings and fly away as an eagle toward heaven.
Jesus said that a man's life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth.
Jesus left his disciples a peace not as the world giveth: let not your heart be troubled.
Jesus said to take no thought for the morrow: sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof.
The Samaritan of the parable bound up a stranger's wounds and paid for his keep. Does detachment from the world free a person for that, or risk passing by on the other side?
Jesus said that no man who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God.
James traces wars and fightings to the lusts that war within: ye desire to have, and cannot obtain.
The guests in the parable all made excuse: one had bought a piece of ground, another five yoke of oxen.
The Qur'an says of the heedless that they know only some appearance of the life of the world.
The Qur'an puts it in a single line: there is no god save him, and everything will perish save his countenance.
Jesus told Martha that she was troubled about many things, but one thing is needful.
The Qur'an says that every soul will taste of death, and calls the life of this world but comfort of illusion.
Plato pictures people chained in a den who take the shadows before them for the whole of reality.
Paul advises using this world as not abusing it, for the fashion of this world passeth away.
Tagore says deliverance is not for him in renunciation: he feels freedom in a thousand bonds of delight. If the world was made for knowing its Maker, is it a veil or a window?
Paul says that to be carnally minded is death, but to be spiritually minded is life and peace.
Paul counted all things but loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ.
The Qur'an says: rivalry in worldly increase distracteth you, until ye come to the graves.
A psalm asks: so teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom.
A psalmist asks: whom have I in heaven but thee? and there is none upon earth that I desire beside thee.
Isaiah describes a land full of silver and gold, with no end of treasures, and full of idols.
Haggai tells a busy people that they earn wages to put into a bag with holes.
Some of Jesus' own disciples said: this is an hard saying; who can hear it?
Amos cried woe to them that are at ease in Zion, and trust in the mountain of Samaria.
Herrick advised: gather ye rosebuds while ye may, for old time is still a-flying. Is love of ease folly, or one honest answer to a short life?
In the parable a rich man fared sumptuously every day while a beggar lay at his gate full of sores.
The merchant in the parable, finding one pearl of great price, went and sold all that he had and bought it.
A psalm says that man's days are as grass; the wind passes over it, and it is gone.
The Preacher made great works, gardens and treasures, and found no profit under the sun.
Jesus explained the seed among thorns: the care of this world and the deceitfulness of riches choke the word.
Isaiah says that the ox knoweth his owner, but Israel doth not know, my people doth not consider.
Jeremiah says the people have forsaken the fountain of living waters, and hewed out broken cisterns that can hold no water.
Those bidden to the king's wedding feast would not come, and went their ways, one to his farm, another to his merchandise.
Arnold heard the sea of faith, once at the full, in a long withdrawing roar.
Marx called religion the sigh of the oppressed creature and the opium of the people. Is turning from the world an awakening, or can it be a sedative?
Paul reminds Timothy that we brought nothing into this world, and it is certain we can carry nothing out.
Montesquieu's Persian visitor wrote of Paris that he had not yet seen anyone walking: they run, they fly.
The Qur'an asks that ye grieve not for what has escaped you, nor exult because of what has been given.
Elizabeth Barrett Browning wrote that earth is crammed with heaven, and every common bush afire with God. Is the world unworthy of joy, or is the fault in who looks?
The Qur'an says: know that the life of this world is only play, and idle talk, and pageantry.
Jesus said that whoever does not forsake all that he has cannot be his disciple.
Hebrews says: here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come.
Jesus was shown all the kingdoms of the world and their glory, and refused them.
Job says that his days are swifter than a weaver's shuttle, and are spent without hope.
A psalmist would rather be a doorkeeper in the house of his God than dwell in the tents of wickedness.
Thoreau went to the woods to live deliberately, to front only the essential facts of life.
Paul wrote to Rome that now it is high time to awake out of sleep.
Proverbs says: better is little with the fear of the Lord than great treasure and trouble therewith.
Hebrews recalls Esau, who for one morsel of meat sold his birthright, and afterward found no way back.
Ecclesiastes says that he that loveth silver shall not be satisfied with silver.
Isaiah says that all flesh is grass, and all its goodliness as the flower of the field.
The Dhammapada says: give up what is before, give up what is behind, give up what is in the middle.
Paul says: I am crucified with Christ; nevertheless I live, yet not I.
Milton could not praise a fugitive and cloistered virtue that never sallies out to meet her adversary. Does dying to the world mean leaving it, or meeting it differently?
Ecclesiastes watches the sun rise and go down, and the wind return again according to his circuits.
The Wisdom of Solomon says to God: thou lovest all the things that are, and abhorrest nothing which thou hast made. If so, how can the world debar anyone from him?
A psalmist says: one thing have I desired of the Lord, that will I seek after.
Jesus said that strait is the gate and narrow is the way that leads to life, and few there be that find it.
Paul asks the Romans not to be conformed to this world, but transformed by the renewing of their mind.
Jesus asked what it shall profit a man if he gain the whole world and lose his own soul.
Khayyam says the lion and the lizard keep the courts where Jamshyd gloried and drank deep.
Khayyam asks only verses, bread, wine and a companion, and calls the wilderness paradise enough. What is lost if happiness is sought only from the other world?
A psalm says that every man walks in a vain shew: he heaps up riches, and knows not who shall gather them.
Thomas à Kempis wrote that all is vanity except to love God and only to serve him.
Ecclesiastes also says it is good and comely to eat and drink and enjoy the good of one's labour, for it is his portion. Is every pleasure a distraction?
